title: Japan's draft AI law outline: attack safeguards, incident reports and penalties
excerpt: A Japanese government working group has seen a draft outline that would require advanced AI providers to guard against cyberattacks, report serious risks, and face penalties if they ignore orders.

sources.title: Nippon.com (Jiji Press): Japan to Revise AI Law to Introduce Penalties
Startup Fortune: Japan's draft AI law would fine foreign AI companies that defy its orders
CASRAI: Japan Outlines AI Law Bill With Penalties
Chip Dispatch: Japan drafts AI rules with 100 million yen fines and ministry inspections

body_html:
Japan's government has set out, for the first time in writing, how it wants to give its AI law teeth. On Friday 27 November 2026, a working group under the government's AI strategy panel was presented with a draft outline that would require providers of advanced AI services to take steps against cyberattacks and other serious harms, and would allow penalties for providers that ignore government orders. The outline is not yet a bill, and no bill text has been published.

Humasure reported on 12 November that officials were considering such powers. The new draft adds detail on duties, enforcement steps and timing.

What Japan's AI law does today

Japan's current AI law, known in English as the AI Promotion Act, was passed by parliament in May 2025. It mainly aims to promote AI research and use. It lets the government investigate problems and give guidance, but it contains no penalties, and its powers are widely described as weak. Jiji Press, Japan's news agency, reported that the new outline is meant to change that.

What the draft outline proposes

According to reports on the draft by Jiji Press (as carried by Nippon.com), Startup Fortune and CASRAI:

  • Who is covered: providers of high-performance AI services used by a certain number of people in Japan. No number has been set. Reports say a provider based abroad would not be exempt, and a company that builds a product on another firm's model would not automatically carry that firm's duties.
  • Safety duties: measures under discussion include blocking answers that could help with cyberattacks or with chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear or explosive threats; preventing foreseeable malfunctions; and checking who is using AI with strong cyber capabilities.
  • Reporting: providers would have to report serious harm, or a concrete risk of it, once their own checks find it. CASRAI also reports a duty to report flaws that attackers could exploit. Startup Fortune says the draft notes that other places set deadlines of 15 days or 72 hours, but sets no Japanese deadline yet.
  • Enforcement in steps: the government would first recommend a fix, then order it if the recommendation is ignored without good reason, and penalties would apply if the order is broken. An emergency order that skips the first step is to be considered.
  • Technical help: Japan's AI Safety Institute could be asked to carry out technical investigations.

What is still unknown

The size of the penalties is not settled. The business newspaper Nikkei reported fines of up to 100 million yen (about US$630,000), but Startup Fortune reports that the draft text itself names no amount and says only that it should be set in line with other Japanese digital laws. Reports also differ on on-site inspections: some describe them as planned, while Startup Fortune says the draft only says the need for such a power should be examined.

The government aims to take public comments and then submit a bill to the ordinary session of parliament (the Diet) in 2027, according to Nikkei as reported by Startup Fortune. Details, including reporting deadlines and which services pass the user threshold, would be set later, partly in guidelines.

Why it matters for people staying in charge

The outline centres on one idea: when a powerful AI system creates a serious risk, someone must tell the authorities and someone must fix it. That is D9 Accountable. Blocking help with cyberattacks and checking who uses strong cyber tools are about D6 Secure and supported. Preventing foreseeable malfunctions, and giving a regulator a way to order a fix quickly, support D1 Always stoppable and D2 Bounded autonomy.

Japan is keeping its light, guidance-first approach for most AI while adding binding steps for the most capable systems. Penalties would follow ignored orders or missed reports, not ordinary research or use. Humasure will follow the bill as it takes shape.
